name: Apple cider vinegar for odour

lead: Some people wipe apple cider vinegar on the underarms or body to cut odour and smell fresher. It is a folk remedy tied to natural-grooming culture.

Body odour arises when skin bacteria break down apocrine sweat. Followers say the acetic acid lowers skin pH and makes skin less hospitable to those bacteria. No published study has tested it for odour, and reference sources describe the evidence for its health claims in general as poor.

paras: Users dilute it with water and wipe or dab it on the underarms with a cloth or cotton pad, usually after washing. Some use it in place of a store-bought deodorant. Acid content varies between commercial brands.
Reference sources say applying vinegar to skin may cause burns. Undiluted use, freshly shaved skin and sensitive skin raise the chance of irritation.

angle.text: Folk-remedy followers wipe diluted vinegar on the underarms, believing its acidity reduces odour-causing bacteria and leaves body odour less noticeable. No published study has tested it for this purpose.

lead: Applying apple cider vinegar to the skin, typically the underarms, to reduce body odour is a folk remedy. Apple cider vinegar is about 5% acetic acid in water, made by fermenting apple cider, and is promoted for many health purposes.[1]

Body odour arises mainly when skin bacteria break down secretions from apocrine sweat glands.[2] Believers say the acidity of vinegar suppresses these bacteria; no published trials were found testing apple cider vinegar for this purpose.
Wikipedia reports that evidence for apple cider vinegar's health claims in general is poor and that applying it to skin may cause burns.[1]

paras: Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting apple juice to alcohol and then converting it to acetic acid; unfiltered versions can retain a bacterial biofilm called the mother.[1] The practice of wiping it on skin to deodorise is shared as a home remedy and is part of broader natural-deodorant culture.

Proponents hold that vinegar's acidity lowers skin pH and makes it less hospitable to odour-causing bacteria. Wikipedia's deodorant article describes acid-based products as aiming to preserve the skin's acid mantle, which limits bacterial growth.[3]

Wikipedia reports no high-quality clinical evidence for apple cider vinegar's claimed benefits, and says major health organisations do not recommend it for therapeutic use.[1] No studies of its effect on body odour were found.
Applying it to skin to treat skin conditions may cause burns, and using vinegar as a topical medication is described as hazardous.[1] Commercial brands vary in acid content.[1]

lore.intro: Apple cider vinegar is discussed in natural-grooming communities as a cheap, home remedy for odour. No forum material was available for this entry.

claims.claim: Wiping vinegar on the underarms removes or prevents body odour

timeline.event: A cookbook includes recipes for apple cider vinegar, reflecting its early-1800s popularity.[1]
